newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ABN AMRO still on prowl for U.S. buy.
newsitem.headline: ABN AMRO still on prowl for U.S. buy.

text.p: Expansionary Dutch bank ABN AMRO NV said on Thursday it remained undaunted in its quest to buy a U.S. fund management company despite failing to find a suitable acquisition in the last two years.
Managing board member Rijnhard van Tets said ABN AMRO was prepared to pay between $200 million and $400 million to bolster its underweight position in the huge U.S. pension fund market.
The bank, aiming to double its global funds under management within five years to 240 billion guilders ($141 million), wants a target with between $20 billion and $40 billion of funds.
"We haven't given up hope yet. We have looked at quite a few. But it's difficult because they're expensive," he said in an interview.
"They're often boutique types of businesses with very good professionals who would have difficulty integrating into our organisation."

Van Tets, in charge of investment banking and global clients including asset management, said ABN AMRO had come close in the last two years to making a U.S. acquisition to fill what it sees as a void in its worldwide funds management activites.
He said agreement had not been reached on price and other issues, and added: "We will not dilute our criteria."

Van Tets said U.S. fund management companies were generally sold for 15-20 times net profit, giving buyers an initial return of about five percent, but ABN AMRO had a target of achieving an annual 13 percent return within three years of a purchase.
"We only do that if we can add value to it," he said.
His preference was for an acquisition in the Chicago area, where the bulk of ABN AMRO's U.S. banking operations are based, but he did not preclude other regions of the country.
ABN AMRO currently has $6 billion under management in the United States, or 20 percent of its 50 billion guilders of funds managed outside the Netherlands.
Its U.S. managed funds doubled with the acquisition this year of investment bank Chicago Corp, extending its banking interests in Chicago.
He said, although the United States was the focus, the bank was also looking for a funds management acquisition in Britain, where it could use independent financial agents for sales.
"That potentially is an interesting market for us," Van Tets said.
ABN AMRO has previously been touted as a possible bidder for British merchant bank Schroders Plc, which is strong in funds management.
But van Tets said that, with a market capitalisation of 2.7 billion pounds ($4.21 billion), Schroders represented a "big ticket", adding he understood it was also not for sale.
Analysts believe the Schroder family does not want to sell its controlling stake in the merchant bank.
ABN AMRO bid unsuccessfully for the funds management arm of Barings, the collapsed British merchant bank bought by ABN's Dutch rival Internationale Nederlanden Groep.
Van Tets said ABN AMRO saw funds management as a core activity, providing a stable source of income to offset the volatility of investment banking returns.
Funds management and custody together provide about half of the bank's securities income.
Securities income in 1995 was 2.03 billion guilders, or 12.5 percent of total income.
Despite the acquisition plans, he said most of the planned growth in funds management would be from existing operations.
ABN AMRO's executive vice-president of asset management, Jaap Fieret, said ABN AMRO could use its banking network in 67 countries to sell investment funds.
He said this gave it an advantage over its British and U.S. non-bank rivals in funds management, which lack branches.
"The only thing you need to do is bring in the products," he said.
He said another edge ABN had over its rivals in this field was the size of its capital base, which offered protection to investors.
Van Tets said most medium-sized institutions preferred to deal with a "one-stop-shop", the term used for a bank offering a range of services.
